title: Women on the Mat
bigQuestion: Why did women and girls reach the mat, the ring and the Olympic program later than men, and who opened those doors?

story.title: The New Weight Sheet
story.kicker: One printed page shows who a sport expects to see.
paragraphs: A wrestling official tapes a sheet to the wall beside the scale. It lists weight classes, one per line, with a blank for each wrestler's name. Older sheets from the same sport had only one column of classes. Every name on them belonged to a man or a boy.

This sheet has a second column. Its heading reads women. The classes in it are set at different weights, and the names are new. Some of the wrestlers on it started on boys' teams because no girls' team existed in their school.

A weight sheet looks like paperwork. Yet it decides who may compete, against whom, and for which title. When a governing body adds a column, it admits that a group of athletes belongs in its official records. Before that, those athletes could train but could not win the sport's own championships.

In combat sports, that change came slowly. Women's fencing reached the Olympics in 1924. Women's judo waited until 1992, wrestling until 2004 and boxing until 2012. Each new column followed years of work by athletes, coaches and lawmakers whose names are part of the record.
story.think: What can a weight sheet tell a historian about who a sport included in a given year?

lessons.title: Title IX in 1972
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX, passed in 1972, banned sex discrimination in schools and colleges that receive federal money.
reading: On June 23, 1972, President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972. One short part of that law is called *Title IX*. It says no person may be shut out of a school program because of sex. The rule covers any school or college that takes federal money.

Title IX did not name sports at all. Its authors were thinking about admissions, jobs and classes. Representative Patsy Mink of Hawaii was one of its main authors. After her death in 2002, Congress renamed the law the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.

Schools soon learned that sports counted as an education program. Girls' teams, budgets and coaches began to grow in high schools and colleges. The law became the main tool for *equal opportunity* in American school sport.

words.d: the part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in education programs receiving federal money
a fair chance to take part, without being shut out because of who you are
belonging to the national government of the United States

look.title: The Words of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, Section 901(a)
look.prompt: The law never uses the word sport. Which words in it made schools apply it to teams?

check.q: What does Title IX ban?
choices: Sex discrimination in education programs that get federal money
check.why: Title IX bans sex discrimination in education programs and activities that receive federal money.

check.q: Who was one of the main authors of Title IX?
check.why: Representative Patsy Mink of Hawaii helped write Title IX; the law now carries her name.

check.q: Why did Title IX come to cover school sports?
choices: Sports were named in its first line
Sports counted as an education program
check.why: The law covers any education program, and schools learned that sports were one.

lessons.title: The Contact Sport Exception
lessons.mainIdea: Rules written in 1975 let schools keep separate teams in contact sports, so wrestling and boxing changed slowly.
reading: Title IX needed detailed rules to be enforced. The federal government issued them in 1975. One rule said a school could run separate teams for boys and girls. It also named certain sports as *contact sports*.

The list of contact sports included boxing, wrestling, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball. In a contact sport, a school did not have to let a girl try out for the boys' team. It also did not have to start a girls' team if few girls asked for one.

This *exception* shaped combat sports for decades. Many schools added girls' basketball, which was on the list, because many girls wanted to play. Girls' wrestling grew far later. For years, a girl who wanted to wrestle often had to ask to join the boys' team.

words.d: a sport in which athletes are expected to touch or collide; the 1975 Title IX rules named several
a case a rule leaves out on purpose
a detailed rule a government agency writes to carry out a law

look.title: Two Sports, One List
look.text: Basketball and wrestling were both on the 1975 contact sport list. By the late 1970s, girls' basketball teams were common in American high schools. Girls' wrestling teams were rare until the 2000s.
look.prompt: Both sports were on the same list. What besides the rule could explain the different timing?

check.q: When were the detailed Title IX sports rules issued?
check.why: The federal government issued the detailed Title IX rules in 1975.

check.q: Which of these was on the 1975 contact sport list?
check.why: Wrestling was named as a contact sport, along with boxing, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball.

check.q: What did the contact sport exception allow?
choices: Schools could refuse a girl a place on the boys' team
Schools had to start girls' boxing
check.why: In a contact sport, a school did not have to let a girl try out for the boys' team.

lessons.title: Girls Build Their Own Teams
lessons.mainIdea: Girls' wrestling grew state by state, and college women's wrestling gained NCAA recognition in 2020.
reading: Through the 1980s and 1990s, some American girls wrestled on boys' high school teams. They trained and competed under the boys' *weight classes*. A few won matches at state tournaments. Their results showed coaches that girls wanted the sport.

Some states then created separate girls' championships. Illinois held its first IHSA girls' state finals in the 2021–22 season. Colleges moved too. Several small colleges started women's wrestling teams in the 1990s and 2000s.

In 2020 the NCAA named women's wrestling an *emerging sport*. That label means the NCAA helps colleges add a women's sport that is still growing. It moves a sport toward an official NCAA championship. Girls' and women's wrestling is now one of the fastest growing school sports.

words.d: a group of athletes of about the same body weight who compete against each other
an NCAA label for a growing women's sport that colleges are encouraged to add

check.why: The first IHSA girls' state finals came in the 2021–22 season.

check.q: What does the NCAA label emerging sport mean?
choices: The NCAA helps colleges add a growing women's sport
The sport is only for professionals
check.why: An emerging sport is a growing women's sport the NCAA helps colleges add.

check.q: Before girls' championships existed, how did many girls wrestle?
check.why: Many girls competed on boys' high school teams before separate championships existed.

lessons.title: A Medal Taken Back
lessons.mainIdea: In 1959 Rusty Kanokogi won a judo medal at a YMCA tournament in New York and was made to give it back because she was a woman.
reading: Rena Glickman grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and began judo in the 1950s. People called her *Rusty*. In 1959 she entered a YMCA judo tournament in upstate New York. She wore her hair short, and her team entered her in the men's contest.

Her team won. Then officials learned she was a woman and asked for her medal back. They said the rules did not allow women in the contest. She gave it back, but she did not leave judo. She later trained at the Kodokan in Tokyo and married Ryohei Kanokogi, a judo teacher.

The YMCA's choice shows how a *tournament rule* could close a sport without saying women could not train. Women were welcome in some judo clubs. What they lacked were official contests and titles. In 2008 the YMCA gave Kanokogi a new medal, almost fifty years later.

words.d: a rule a contest's organizers write about who may enter and how winners are named
the Young Men's Christian Association, a group that ran gyms and sports programs
the judo school and headquarters Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882

check.why: After her team won, officials learned she was a woman and asked for the medal back.

check.why: Rena Glickman Kanokogi grew up in Brooklyn, New York.

check.q: When did the YMCA give Kanokogi a new medal?
check.why: In 2008 the YMCA gave her a medal, almost fifty years after the tournament.

lessons.title: A World Title for Women
lessons.mainIdea: In 1980 Kanokogi organized the first women's world judo championships, held at Madison Square Garden in New York.
reading: By the 1970s women's judo contests were growing in Europe, Japan and the Americas. Yet there was no women's *world championship*. Men's world judo championships had been held since 1956. Kanokogi decided to organize a women's one herself.

She raised money, found sponsors and even took out a loan on her home. In November 1980 the first women's world judo championships were held at Madison Square Garden in New York City. Athletes came from many countries. Official medals now existed for women at the world level.

Kanokogi then pressed the International Judo Federation and the International Olympic Committee to add women. Women's judo appeared as a *demonstration event* at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. It became a full medal sport four years later.

words.d: a contest, run by a sport's world federation, that names the best athletes on Earth for that year
an event shown at the Olympics without official medals, often as a test before a sport is added
a person or company that pays toward an event

choices: An event with no official medals, shown at the Games
check.why: A demonstration event is shown at the Olympics without official medals.

lessons.title: A Ceiling on Rank
lessons.mainIdea: For decades Kodokan women stopped at fifth dan; Keiko Fukuda was promoted to sixth dan in 1972 and ninth dan in 2006.
reading: A *dan* is a black-belt rank in judo. Higher numbers mark longer service and greater standing. For decades, women at the Kodokan did not rise above fifth dan. Men with similar years of teaching could go higher.

Keiko Fukuda moved to the United States and taught women's judo in San Francisco from the 1960s. Students and supporters argued that the rank limit was unfair. In 1972 the Kodokan promoted Fukuda to sixth dan. She was the first woman to pass the old limit.

In 2006 the Kodokan made her a ninth dan, the first woman to reach it there. In 2011 USA Judo awarded her tenth dan, its highest rank. She died in 2013. A *rank ceiling* is a quiet kind of exclusion, because it lets people in but stops how far they rise.

words.d: a black-belt rank in judo and other Japanese arts, counted upward from first
a limit on how high a group of people may be promoted
being moved up to a higher rank

look.title: Keiko Fukuda's Promotions

look.prompt: How many years passed between her first promotion past the limit and her ninth dan?

check.why: A dan is a black-belt rank, counted upward from first.

check.q: What happened in 1972?
choices: Fukuda was promoted past the old fifth dan limit
check.why: In 1972 the Kodokan promoted Fukuda to sixth dan, the first woman to pass the limit.

check.q: Why is a rank ceiling a form of exclusion?
choices: It lets people in but limits how far they rise
check.why: A rank ceiling admits people but stops their promotion at a set level.

lessons.title: Barcelona Adds Seven Classes
lessons.mainIdea: When women's judo became a medal sport in 1992, it arrived with seven weight classes, the same number as the men's.
reading: At the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, women's judo held seven *medal events*. The men also had seven. Each event is one weight class with its own gold, silver and bronze medals. Women's judo entered the Games at full size, not as a single trial event.

That choice was not true of every combat sport. Women's wrestling began in 2004 with four classes, while men had more. Women's boxing began in 2012 with only three, against ten for men. The number of classes decides how many women can win medals.

The *Olympic program* is the list of sports and events at one Games. The International Olympic Committee approves it after hearing from each federation. Adding a women's event often meant cutting or reshaping a men's event, because the total number of athletes is capped.

words.d: one contest at the Olympics that awards its own gold, silver and bronze
the list of sports and events held at one Olympic Games

look.title: Women's Medal Events at Each Sport's Debut
look.cite: International Olympic Committee, official results of the 1992, 2000, 2004 and 2012 Games
look.prompt: Which sport let the most women win medals in its first Games? Why might that matter?

check.why: Women's judo arrived at Barcelona with seven weight classes, the same as the men.

check.q: What is the Olympic program?
choices: The list of sports and events at one Games
check.why: The Olympic program lists the sports and events held at one Games.

check.q: Why could adding women's events mean changing men's events?
choices: The total number of athletes is capped

check.why: The IOC caps the number of athletes, so new events often reshape old ones.

lessons.title: Taekwondo Starts Even
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo entered the Olympics in 2000 with four weight classes for women and four for men.
reading: Taekwondo became a full Olympic medal sport at the Sydney Games in 2000. Unlike judo and wrestling, it had women's events from its first medal year. There were four weight classes for women and four for men.

The world body, now called World Taekwondo, had held women's world championships since 1987. So by 2000 there was already a pool of women with international records. The first women's Olympic taekwondo gold medal went to Lauren Burns of Australia, in the lightest class.

Olympic taekwondo has fewer classes than its world championships. Each Olympic class covers a wider *weight range*. That squeeze lets the sport fit inside the Olympic cap while keeping men's and women's events equal in number.

words.d: the span from the lightest to the heaviest body weight allowed in one class
the international federation that runs Olympic-style taekwondo

check.why: Taekwondo became a full medal sport at Sydney in 2000.

check.q: Who won the first women's Olympic taekwondo gold?
check.why: Lauren Burns of Australia won the first women's taekwondo gold in 2000.

lessons.title: Wrestling Waits for Athens
lessons.mainIdea: Women's freestyle wrestling held world championships from 1987 but joined the Olympics only in 2004.
reading: Wrestling was part of the first modern Olympics in 1896. For more than a hundred years, only men wrestled there. Women's wrestling clubs grew in France, Norway, Japan and elsewhere in the 1970s and 1980s.

The world wrestling body held its first women's world championships in 1987, in Norway. The women wrestled *freestyle*, one of the two Olympic styles. Japan, China, the United States and Canada soon built strong women's programs.

Women's freestyle wrestling joined the Olympics at Athens in 2004 with four classes. In 2016 the program changed to six classes for women and six for each men's style. The *gap* between a first world title and a first Olympic medal was seventeen years.

words.d: one of the two Olympic wrestling styles, and the only one women compete in at the Games
the time between two events in a timeline

look.title: Two Dates in Norway and Greece
look.text: 1987: the first women's world wrestling championships are held in Norway. 2004: women wrestle for Olympic medals for the first time, in Athens, Greece, near the site of the ancient Games.
look.prompt: Wrestling was one of the ancient Greek contests. What does it mean that women first wrestled for Olympic medals in Greece in 2004?

check.q: When did women's wrestling join the Olympics?
check.why: Women's freestyle wrestling joined at Athens in 2004.

check.q: Which style do women wrestle at the Olympics?
check.why: Women compete in freestyle, one of the two Olympic wrestling styles.

check.q: What changed in 2016?
choices: Women's wrestling grew to six classes
check.why: In 2016 the program gave women six classes, the same as each men's style.

lessons.title: The Sumo Ring and a Medical Emergency
lessons.mainIdea: Professional sumo keeps women off its ring, and a 2018 emergency in Maizuru made that rule a national debate in Japan.
reading: The *dohyō* is the raised clay ring of sumo. The Japan Sumo Association, which runs professional sumo, does not let women step onto it. The association links the rule to tradition and to the ring's role in Shinto ceremonies. Critics in Japan call it sex discrimination.

On April 4, 2018, the mayor of Maizuru collapsed while giving a speech on a dohyō during a touring event. Several women from the crowd, including a nurse, climbed up to give him first aid. A referee announced over the speakers that women should leave the ring.

The association's chairman apologized and said life-saving care came first. Earlier, Osaka's governor, Fusae Ohta, had asked in 2000 to present a trophy on the ring herself and was refused. Meanwhile, amateur women's sumo holds its own contests and world championships.

words.d: the raised clay ring where sumo matches are held
the body that runs professional sumo in Japan
for athletes who are not paid to compete

look.title: Tradition and a Life
look.text: A mayor falls on a sumo ring. Women trained in first aid climb up to help. An announcer asks them to leave. Days later, the sport's chairman says saving a life comes first.
look.prompt: The rule and the apology point in different directions. How would you explain why the rule has lasted?

check.why: Fusae Ohta, governor of Osaka, asked to present a trophy and was refused.

lessons.title: Fencing One Weapon at a Time
lessons.mainIdea: Women's Olympic fencing began with foil in 1924, but épée waited until 1996 and sabre until 2004.
reading: Modern fencing uses three weapons: foil, épée and sabre. Each has its own rules about where a touch counts. Men fenced all three at the Olympics from the early 1900s. Women's fencing began with *foil* at the Paris Games of 1924.

For seventy years, foil was the only weapon women fenced at the Olympics. Many officials of the time judged it the proper weapon for women. Women's *épée* joined at Atlanta in 1996. Women's *sabre* joined at Athens in 2004.

Fencing shows that a sport can admit women early and still limit them. The first door opened in 1924. The last one opened eighty years later. Today women fence all three weapons, in both individual and team events.

words.d: a light fencing weapon; the first one women fenced at the Olympics, in 1924
a heavier fencing weapon; women's Olympic épée began in 1996
a fencing weapon scored with the edge as well as the point; women's Olympic sabre began in 2004
